Well, I don't care for most social/casual shit, but a Minecraft or Terraria server with friends and acquaintances is a good time, and CAN be casual. For non-video games, I play dominoes. Or more precisely, domino island solitaire.

[Edit] Scratch that. Domino island solitaire requires a lot of thinking if you want to get optimal solutions.

If you want a good casual co-op party game that a bunch of people can enjoy which is quite social I'd suggest Spaceteam. This is a phone/tablet game, but try not to let that color your judgement before trying it. it'll work on ios or android (cross platform play supported) and is multiplayer for 2 - 8 people at the same time. It's realtime not turn based, and there is a lot of yelling absurd things involved. The premise of the game is that you and your friends are piloting a spaceship which is falling apart.

Each person has a randomly generated control panel with a variety of knobs, switches, sliders, and buttons that are labeled is ridiculous ways. They must be manipulated to keep the spaceship alive. Every player gets orders which may be relevant to any player in the game. This leads to the shouting part as they try to relay the orders to the other players. The more the orders get completed successfully, the greater your chances of your group's survival.

I'd suggest bringing beer, wine, or whatever your alcohol of choice is. This is not an online multiplayer game, people are expected to be in the same room and each player needs their own phone or tablet to join in. I usually bring a spare tablet just in case someone doesn't have one, but most people will have at least their own smartphone so it usually works out. Bluetooth and Wifi are both supported, so a wifi infrastructure is not necessary making it playable pretty much anywhere.

Oh. My. God. Don't like your job? Quit!

I would love to have a job programming. I would love to have a job where I get paid for sitting at my computer 12 hours a day.

developers sleeping at their desks, eating nothing but noodles, and forgetting their families

Clearly these things are worth what you're being paid (in salary, benefits, perks, "culture") otherwise you wouldn't be doing them.

I think most of the people who work in the games industry are aware that the job is tough. It's miles away from the 'Happy Happy Joy Joy' most outsiders probably think of when talking about developing games, essentially an amusement product. I do some QA volunteer work for a small indie studio as a hobby, and even so (as someone who can just chip in and out of the 'job' whenever I feel like it), I know that the working conditions especially during the crunch time can be nightmarish - you never have as much of a budget as you want to, you never have as much time as you want to, and god help you if you have a publisher breathing down your neck who doesn't give a shit about the game but simply wants the finished product so he can make money.

That being said, I think you need to differentiate between scenarios where developers accept this as being a (however nasty) necessity in game development, and scenarios like those the wife of a certain EA employee described. It's one thing to get your hands dirty during work, but another thing entirely to slave away for developers who arbitrarily cut or expand team size, demand unrealistic shipping dates, etc.

USNR Lt. Walter Chewning climbs onto the burning fuel tank of a Hellcat fighter to rescue a pilot who crashed on the deck of the USS Enterprise and was trapped in his cockpit. Pacific Ocean. 1943.

U.S. Navy Grumman F6F-3 Hellcat on a routine training exercise off of USS Enterprise en route to Makin Atoll, piloted by Ensign (later Lieutenant) Byron Milton Johnson of Potter, Nebraska, suffers engine problems, makes emergency landing, catches 3 wire on his third attempt, slams into deck and ends up with port landing gear leg in the port catwalk near 20mm (.78 caliber) Oerlikon anti-aircraft guns.

Airframe rests on belly tank, which begins to leak, propeller blades turning against deck edge emit sparks which set fuel alight. Hard landing jams canopy, retaining pin sheared. Lieutenant (later Lieutenant Commander) Walter Lewis Chewning of Cynwyd, Pennsylvania, a new catapult officer, rescues Johnson, stepping on the burning tank to reach the cockpit.

Chewning was awarded the Navy and Marine Corps Medal for his actions. The commander of VF-2's Air Group, famed fighter pilot Edward "Butch" O'Hare recommended that night that all pilots drop their external tank before landing to prevent such an accident repeating.
